claims.text: AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles lose sub-5 nm particles during heating.
Au and Cu segregate to the surfaces of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during heating.
Surface-energy minimization, rather than sluggish diffusion, drives the particle loss and Au/Cu segregation.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-10 nm particles produces steep surface-energy gradients.
These surface-energy gradients override entropic stabilization of the FCC structure.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
The surface-energy differences cause Au and Cu to segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu have lower cohesive energies than the other alloy constituents.
Au and Cu have higher vapor pressures at elevated temperatures than the other alloy constituents.
Surface-enriched Au and Cu preferentially evaporate because of their cohesive energies and vapor pressures.
Preferential evaporation causes particle shrinkage.
The proposed process widens the nanoparticle size distribution.
The proposed process reshapes particles from elliptical to spherical geometries.
Surface diffusion becomes sufficiently active at approximately 600-700 K to enable rapid segregation and evaporation.
Icosahedral particles possess higher-energy surface facets than truncated-octahedral particles dominated by lower-energy {111} facets.
Icosahedral particles segregate and evaporate faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
The mechanism is dominant for particles smaller than 10 nm.
The mechanism is negligible for particles larger than 50 nm because bulk thermodynamics dominate.
The PLD-grown nanoparticles initially exhibit an FCC structure.
Atomistic simulations containing surface-energy terms but excluding sluggish-diffusion effects will reproduce the experimentally observed phase separation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the surface-energy mechanism does not require sluggish diffusion to be inactive, whereas the proposed simulations explicitly exclude sluggish-diffusion effects. Such simulations cannot directly establish that the mechanism works without requiring those effects to be inactive or absent.
